title: AI Adoption: Course Completion Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: A marketing page claims the organization uses machine learning to guarantee a safety step in every order, and the quality team cannot demonstrate it. What rule should govern AI capability claims?
options: Claims need review only after a regulator requests supporting documentation
No AI capability claim ships without evidence attached that the team can produce
A claim is acceptable if the vendor's own documentation supports the functionality
Claims about operations sit outside governance, which covers customer-facing tools
questions.explanation: A capability claim is testable, and the test is whether the organization can produce the evidence behind it. Claims that cannot be demonstrated are misrepresentations, whatever the intention behind them.

questions.question: Why end a redundant contract at its renewal date rather than immediately?
options: Vendors will not discuss a migration until the existing agreement has fully expired
A forced mid-contract switch pays twice for the same job and makes consolidation painful
Users need a full year to learn a replacement before the old tool can be removed
The renewal date is the only point at which a vendor is legally permitted to delete company data
questions.explanation: Contracts end on dates, which is when ending one is cheap and starting another is negotiable; cutting early means paying both vendors for the same work.

questions.question: What makes a stage gate a real decision rather than a review meeting?
options: The gate is held on a fixed date each quarter with exactly the same set of attendees present
The project team prepares its own numbers and presents them to the executive sponsor
The gate can be skipped whenever the pilot showed strong enthusiasm among its users
The criteria and the evidence were named before the project started, in one shared pack
questions.explanation: A gate decides only when the criteria and the evidence were agreed in advance and both sides read the same numbers; otherwise the meeting argues about data.

questions.question: Why buy fewer seats than the number of eligible employees at the start?
options: Eligibility is a permission, and a waitlist measures who actually intends to use the tool
Buying fewer seats lowers the per-seat price that the vendor is willing to offer
Eligible employees rarely want the tool, so most of them would never log in anyway
Seat counts must almost always stay below total headcount because of standard contract terms
questions.explanation: Adoption is a behavior while eligibility is only a permission, so buying to eligibility turns a behavior question into a sunk cost and removes the waitlist that shows which teams are pulling.

questions.question: A document lists customer names, account numbers, and contract terms. How should it be treated?
options: Public, because it is ordinary business paperwork that anyone could see
Internal Only, because it stays inside the company
Confidential, because disclosure could harm customers and the firm
Restricted, because all customer data counts as a trade secret
questions.explanation: Confidential data covers customer records, contracts, and financial material whose disclosure would cause harm. Restricted is a narrower tier reserved for trade secrets, source code, and regulated personal information.

questions.question: Why pair a north-star metric with a guardrail metric?
options: To give leadership a second number to review alongside the first
To catch the case where the north-star is met by cutting quality
To replace the north-star whenever it stops moving
To measure usage more precisely than the dashboard does
questions.explanation: Any measure turned into a target invites the cheap path, so a guardrail threshold shows when the gain is being bought with worse quality.

questions.question: An incident is confirmed. What is the first job?
options: Find the root cause so the fix can be designed before anything else
Notify every affected customer before any internal step is taken
Stop the harm from spreading, then work out why it happened
Document the timeline in full detail for the post-incident review
questions.explanation: Containment comes before diagnosis because the damage keeps accruing while you investigate; understanding the cause can wait until the bleeding has stopped.

questions.question: What separates a running adoption program from a rollout?
options: It has no finish line and keeps adapting as tools and the business change
It has a fixed timeline, a defined deliverable, and closes once the tool goes live
It runs as a single training event with a completion date
It ends when licenses are purchased and access is granted
questions.explanation: A rollout is a bounded project with a clear deliverable and an end, while a program is the ongoing work of sustaining use, measuring value, and governing risk.

questions.question: What shows that remediation worked, rather than that the symptom merely stopped?
options: The immediate problem has stopped and no complaint has arrived
The same failure could not happen again through the same path
The vendor has confirmed the model was updated to a newer one
The post-incident review document has been written and filed
questions.explanation: Fixing the root cause, or adding a check that catches that class of error, is what prevents a repeat; a quiet week only means nobody has noticed yet.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an adoption baseline?
options: A snapshot of what is actually in use, where, and on what data
A forecast of how much AI use each department will add next year
A list of the tools the company has officially approved for staff
A plan for which workflows the program will target next
questions.explanation: A baseline records ground truth about current use, and every later decision about goals, budget, and policy is measured against it.

questions.question: Which term matters most before routing confidential material through an AI tool?
options: The limit on the vendor's total liability across the contract term
The notice period the vendor must give before retiring a model
Whether the vendor may train on your inputs and outputs
The support hours, the escalation path, and the named contact
questions.explanation: If the vendor may train on what you send, confidential material can end up inside a model later served to other customers, so this term decides most of the data-side risk.

questions.question: A team saves ten hours a week with AI but takes on no additional work. How should that saving be booked?
options: As a realized saving, because the hours saved were measured against a before baseline
As a risk reduction, because the team has more room to absorb future demand
As revenue uplift, because the freed hours give the team capacity it can sell
As unused capacity, since no revenue, avoided cost, or reduced risk was shown
questions.explanation: Saved time becomes value only when it is redeployed into revenue, avoided cost, or reduced risk; otherwise it is capacity the company paid for and never used.

questions.question: An employee pastes a confidential schedule into an unapproved assistant and reports it. What decides whether the response takes minutes or weeks?
options: Whether the tool blocks pastes of confidential content at the client level
Whether the employee had completed the data handling training for their role
Whether the vendor's contract requires the customer to notify it within a defined window
Whether the path was decided in advance: who is told, what is recorded, and how fast
questions.explanation: An incident path is a decision made in advance: who to tell first, what gets recorded, what the external obligation is, and how quickly. Without one, the delay measures the absence of a policy rather than the size of the incident.

questions.question: How does provider risk differ from model risk?
options: Model risk is about price, while provider risk is about licensing terms
Model risk disappears once a newer model is released by the same provider
A model can be swapped, but a provider outage defeats any replacement
Provider risk ends when the contract names a fixed model version
questions.explanation: A model is replaceable in principle, but when the company serving it goes down, changes terms, or exits, no substitute model rescues you at that layer.

questions.question: Two organizations buy the same AI tool and get very different results. What best explains the gap?
options: One bought a more capable model and paid a higher license price
One redesigned the workflow around the tool instead of bolting it on
One gave the tool to a much larger number of employees across several teams
One ran a longer training program before the launch
questions.explanation: Value is a property of the redesigned workflow, not of the model, so the same tool performs differently depending on whether the work around it changed.

questions.question: Why does a survey of employees give weak evidence about time saved?
options: People judge their own speed poorly and enthusiasm colors the answer
Surveys cannot be run anonymously inside a large company
Employees almost always understate the time they save on a repeated task
Time saved cannot be measured in any reliable way at all
questions.explanation: A feeling of being faster tracks mood and enthusiasm, so a before-and-after measurement of the same defined task is stronger evidence than self-report.

questions.question: Why does a small evaluation set built from your own workflow do work that a published benchmark cannot?
options: It contains enough tasks to rank two close models with statistical confidence
It is maintained by the vendor, so it tracks the exact model versions that you use
It removes the need to record the cost of each task alongside the pass rate
It measures the change on your own tasks and catches a regression that scores hide
questions.explanation: Published scores measure a vendor's chosen tasks and have begun to saturate, while an owned set of real tasks shows whether a change helped your work and what it now costs. Its job is to catch a large regression or gain, not to rank two close models.

questions.question: What separates real AI governance from theater?
options: Someone independent holds the authority to stop a system and can actually exercise it
The organization maintains a registry, dashboards, and a written policy for AI use
The council meets every month and includes legal, security, and finance leads
Every use case is reviewed by a full committee before any tool at all can be purchased
questions.explanation: Registries, dashboards, and policies create visibility; governance exists only when a named person with standing can shut a misbehaving system down.

questions.question: How should the interval between audits be set?
options: Every system is checked on the same annual cycle so the process stays simple
High-risk systems are checked more often, and every interval has a scheduled date
The interval stays open so checks happen whenever someone notices a problem worth raising
Only the cheapest tools are checked, since waste is the main risk with AI tools
questions.explanation: Review intensity follows risk, and the real requirement is a date on the calendar, because a check that depends on memory is not a cadence.

questions.question: When triaging a discovered tool, what should drive the governance decision?
options: How much the tool costs and whether a budget line exists for it
Which department adopted it and how senior its sponsor is
What data the tool handles and whether that data may leave
How popular the tool is among staff who have tried it
questions.explanation: Triage is a data question, not a popularity or budget question: what category of data the tool sees, and whether that category may go to a provider you never vetted.

questions.question: What should happen after a pilot clears its technical checkpoints?
options: Full rollout to the whole organization, since a cleared pilot has proven the value
A pause until the vendor ships a more accurate version of the underlying model
An MVP phase with live but limited exposure and a gate on safety, adoption, and impact
A second pilot in an entirely different department to confirm that the same results will repeat
questions.explanation: Proof of feasibility is not proof of scale; the next step puts the system into real workflows with limited exposure and tests safety, adoption, and impact.

questions.question: Why does a long notice period combined with an auto-renewing term matter more than it looks?
options: It locks the price for the life of the agreement, so no increase can land
It transfers liability for inaccurate outputs from the buyer to the vendor
It removes the vendor's right to retire or replace the model mid-term
It can narrow the days each year when leaving is actually possible
questions.explanation: If notice must be given far ahead of a renewal that happens on its own, the usable escape window shrinks to a few weeks a year and is easy to miss entirely.

questions.question: What does over-governance do to an organization?
options: It raises the cost of compliance but reliably lowers the number of serious incidents
It slows decisions until teams route around it and use unsanctioned tools instead
It moves risk decisions from managers to the council, which is where they belong
It makes the policy shorter, since fewer use cases survive the review process
questions.explanation: Governance calibrated slower than the technology pushes people back to unsanctioned tools, so the shadow use it was meant to stop spreads further.

questions.question: Why is a speed gain on its own an unsafe measure of AI value?
options: Speed gains reported by users are usually exaggerated by enthusiasm
Speed only matters for engineering and support work
Faster work on a bad fit just reaches a wrong answer sooner
Tool speed varies from one day to the next and is hard to compare
questions.explanation: Measuring speed without quality rewards finishing sooner even on tasks the tool handles badly, which produces confident errors at higher throughput.

questions.question: A use case is ready to move from a pilot to organization-wide use. Which set of conditions belongs in the scale gate?
options: Executive support, a vendor roadmap commitment, a launch date, and a completed training session
Quality on your own tasks, a named owner, a support path, and a defensible unit cost
A pilot group of at least fifty users, two quarters of data, and an approved invoice
A written policy, a communications plan, a committee vote, and a budget line
questions.explanation: A scale gate is what turns a pilot into a decision: quality measured on your own tasks, a named business owner, a support path that exists on a bad day, and a unit cost you can defend against the manual alternative. Without those four lines a use case goes wide on enthusiasm.

questions.question: An audit that starts from opinions rather than records is weak because:
options: It takes far longer to run than an audit built on a fixed list of specific evidence pulls
It duplicates work that continuous monitoring already does in real time
It measures whether people objected in a meeting rather than whether the rules held
It cannot be placed on a calendar, so it tends to happen only once a year
questions.explanation: An audit is only as strong as the records it compares against expectations; without named evidence it becomes a discussion about intentions.

questions.question: A team member doubts the tool works and asks for evidence that it saves time. Which reaction is this?
options: Fear, which calls for reassurance that nobody in the team will lose their role
Skepticism, which calls for specific evidence of what the tool does
Fear, which calls for letting the person set the adoption pace
Skepticism, which calls for restating the rollout plan more firmly
questions.explanation: Skepticism is a rational doubt, and it answers to evidence, provided the evidence is specific and honest. Reassurance aimed at feelings does not resolve a question about whether the tool actually works.

questions.question: Which reading suggests momentum rather than a novelty spike?
options: High reach with high churn among people who tried it once
Steady reach with low churn and the same people returning
A sharp rise in sign-ups during the first week
A large number of one-time trials across many different departments
questions.explanation: Momentum shows up in depth and retention, the same people coming back, while a spike shows up in breadth and churn.

questions.question: What does keeping your AI work portable mean in practice?
options: Store outputs wherever the provider's interface keeps them
Keep prompts and outputs in formats you control and can export
Rely on the provider to migrate your data if it retires a model
Copy everything to a second provider every month to stay current
questions.explanation: Portability lives in the artifacts you would have to move: prompts written to travel, and outputs saved in a standard format somewhere you control.

questions.question: What is the difference between a deprecated model and a retired one?
options: A deprecated model answers at a higher price, and a retired model answers as before
Deprecation applies to preview models, and retirement applies to general releases
A deprecated model still answers but has an end date, and a retired one returns an error
Deprecation can be reversed at the vendor's discretion, and retirement can never be reversed
questions.explanation: A deprecated model keeps serving existing deployments while new use is closed, and its end date is the signal to schedule a migration. A retired model fails every request, so it should never arrive as news.

questions.question: A customer-facing assistant gives a customer a policy answer that contradicts the written contract. Leadership argues the statement belongs to the tool vendor because the product is third-party. What is the correct position?
options: The vendor is answerable, since the answer was generated from its model
No liability arises if the customer could have read the written contract before ordering
The statement the system makes is the company's statement, whoever produced it
Liability depends on whether the page is static or interactive for the customer
questions.explanation: Responsibility for what a system says does not move because a machine produced the statement, and treating the tool as a separate party has been rejected where it was tested. The answer a customer relies on is the organization's answer.

questions.question: Why does a clause saying you own the output not guarantee you can stop a competitor copying it?
options: Because a contract can assign rights but cannot create a copyright
Because ownership clauses only apply to works registered with the office
Because vendors keep ownership of anything their models produce
Because copyright protects ideas rather than the expression of them
questions.explanation: A contract can only pass along rights the provider actually holds; where no human authored the expression, there is no copyright for the clause to hand over.

questions.question: A connector is built on one shared service credential so the pilot can start faster. What problem does that design create?
options: The assistant answers slowly, because every request is re-authorized against the same account
Usage reporting becomes unreliable, because all questions arrive under one identity
The assistant can reach records that the person asking is not allowed to open
The connection fails whenever the credential owner is unavailable or changes roles
questions.explanation: A shared credential carries whatever access the account holds rather than the access of the person asking, so the assistant can surface records a user cannot open. Mirroring each user's permissions is the safer default, and a connection that cannot refuse a request is not ready.

questions.question: A strong result published months ago is still posted after the tool failed to scale. What is the right response?
options: Leave the old figure up because it was accurate when it was published
Remove the old figure quietly so that nobody notices the change
Revalidate published claims on a schedule and correct them openly
Withdraw every claim the program has made and start over
questions.explanation: Stale claims, more than new ones, cause most of the damage once conditions change. A scheduled review that revalidates or corrects published numbers keeps the record accurate at low cost.

questions.question: How does a proof of concept differ from a demo?
options: A demo is free to watch, while a proof of concept is always a paid trial
A demo proves the tool works, while a proof of concept only gathers opinions
A demo uses the vendor's example, while a proof of concept uses your own
A demo is run on site, while a proof of concept is run by the vendor remotely
questions.explanation: A demo shows the vendor's chosen case, which is built to look good; a proof of concept measures the tool against your data and a success bar you set beforehand.

questions.question: What distinguishes a champion from a power user?
options: A champion has the deeper technical command of the tool and all of its settings
A champion brings trust and influence, while a power user brings deep expertise
A champion writes policy, while a power user trains new staff
A champion is a manager, while a power user is an individual contributor
questions.explanation: A champion moves adoption through trust and example, while a power user moves it through practical command of a specific tool and workflow.

questions.question: A team collects detailed usage data for a quarter and changes nothing. What is missing?
options: A larger and more representative sample gathered before conclusions
A clearer dashboard that presents the same usage data in a more compelling way
The close: a visible change from the signals, with people told what changed
More frequent surveys to confirm what the usage data already shows
questions.explanation: Collecting signals without acting on them is data hoarding, and people stop supplying signal when nothing changes. The visible change plus telling people what it was and why keeps the loop alive.

questions.question: A program needs training to keep serving new hires without the adoption owner running every session. Which structure does that?
options: Reusable material delivered by local champions on a repeating cadence
The owner running more sessions each quarter as headcount grows
New hires watching a recording of the original launch workshop
Requiring the launch module to be finished within the first working week
questions.explanation: Material is written once, delivery passes to champions who know the local work, and the reinforcement cadence runs without the owner. That division of labor is what lets training scale with headcount.

questions.question: Why does requiring a human check on every output weaken supervision?
options: It slows the workflow enough that people stop using the tool
Attention flattens, so the outputs that matter get the same glance
It removes the reviewer's authority to reject an output they disagree with
It conflicts with the vendor's terms for enterprise deployments
questions.explanation: People cannot sustain attention across a stream of items they mostly do not need to care about. A blanket check turns review into ritual, so the few outputs that need real judgment get no more scrutiny than the rest.

questions.question: A leader proposes the share of employees who touched AI this month as the north-star. Why is that a poor choice?
options: It counts activity rather than value, so it can climb while no work improves
It is too expensive to collect and report on every month across the whole company
It covers too few employees to be meaningful for the program
It changes too often to track across a quarter
questions.explanation: A north-star has to capture value, and a measure of who touched the tool says nothing about whether anyone's work got faster or better.

questions.question: A high-consequence tool is signed and running. Who staffs the human oversight and monitoring?
options: The vendor, because it built the model and operates the servers
Nobody in particular, as long as the tool meets its accuracy claims
The vendor and the buyer share it equally under standard terms
The deploying organization, which must staff those duties itself
questions.explanation: Oversight duties attach to the organization that puts the system to use, so they land on your payroll after the signature no matter what the contract says about vendor liability.

questions.question: An employee cannot name the data level or say which tool is approved. What should the routine tell them?
options: Paste a short excerpt and check whether the output looks correct
Ask a colleague and proceed if that colleague believes it is fine
Use the tool anyway and delete the conversation afterward
Treat the data as restricted and stop before anything is pasted
questions.explanation: The routine turns an unclear case into a safe default, so unclear data is treated as restricted. Confidential material leaves only when someone has deliberately established that an approved tool and path make it safe.

questions.question: Why should a pilot's kill criteria be written when it is approved rather than when it disappoints?
options: It moves the decision onto a number agreed in advance, so that stopping is not an argument
It guarantees the metric will hold, because everyone knows the threshold from the start
It removes the need for a named decision maker, since the numbers decide on their own
It lets the pilot skip the business case entirely, because thresholds replace the financial analysis
questions.explanation: A metric, a threshold, and a date agreed at approval move the weight of the decision from the person who championed the idea to a number nobody has to argue about later. Stopping then costs a decision rather than a fight.

questions.question: A target doubles a number with no reading of where the program starts. What is missing?
options: A longer deadline for the team to reach the number without extra staff
A larger team to carry the work
A baseline reading, without which the target is only a guess
A bigger budget for tool licenses
questions.explanation: Without a baseline the target cannot be judged as ambitious or achievable, which turns a decision into a guess.

questions.question: Why is treating the first month as the whole change effort a mistake?
options: People need at least a full year before any new behavior becomes an automatic routine
Habit research puts the median well past a month, so the effort must continue
Training sessions usually take longer than a month to schedule
Tools are typically replaced within a month of going live
questions.explanation: Automaticity takes far longer than a launch window, and the dip after the novelty fades is exactly when reinforcement matters most.

questions.question: Which pricing shape gives the buyer a budgetable base while protecting the vendor as adoption grows?
options: A flat per-seat fee with no usage component charged at all
A pure per-token meter with no base subscription fee attached
A base plus allowance, with overage metered per unit
A per-outcome fee charged only when a defined result happens
questions.explanation: A base covers predictable usage and gives finance a fixed number, while the metered overage covers volume beyond the allowance so the vendor is not exposed to runaway cost.

questions.question: Which item is a financial outcome rather than a leading indicator of activity?
options: A measured reduction in cost per resolved support ticket
The share of employees who used the tool at least once last week
The average number of prompts each active user sends to the tool per day
The hours employees report saving through the tool each week
questions.explanation: Adoption, prompt volume, and self-reported time saved show momentum; only revenue uplift, cost reduction, and risk reduction are outcomes a board can treat as return.

questions.question: What separates a near miss from an incident, and why does it matter?
options: It caused no harm, and it flags where the next failure is likely
It caused limited harm, and it must be reported to a regulator
It is a vendor failure, and logging it belongs to the vendor
It is a false alarm, and it can be safely ignored once it is found
questions.explanation: A near miss is a harm that was caught before it landed, which makes it the cheapest evidence you will ever get about where a real failure is forming.

questions.question: Why does the baseline come before the policy when an adoption plan is assembled?
options: Because the finance lead has to sign off on the policy before it is written
Because the prohibited list is copied directly from the baseline inventory
Because controls written before the organization has been counted aim at nothing
Because the approving group has to approve the baseline before any policy text is drafted
questions.explanation: Controls and thresholds only mean something against a known starting position, so a plan written policy first and baseline last produces rules aimed at nothing. Counting what the organization operates also produces the list of questions nobody can answer, which is the most useful page in the exercise.

questions.question: Why does one intensive workshop produce weaker long-term retention than short sessions repeated over several weeks?
options: Short sessions cover less content, so each piece is easier to absorb
Workshops create pressure that blocks people from learning the material
Spacing repetitions over time builds stronger memory than massing them
Repeated sessions are easier to fit around busy working weeks
questions.explanation: Spaced practice beats massed practice because each repetition lands after some forgetting has occurred. A single sitting feels efficient, but retention fades once people leave the room.

questions.question: Three candidate connections compete for one quarter of engineering time. How should they be ordered?
options: By announced business value, largest first, so the program can show results early
By the size of the team that requested each one, so the loudest need goes first
By reversibility of the worst likely failure first, then by the population that benefits
By technical difficulty, easiest first, so that the team builds confidence before harder work
questions.explanation: Rank by how easily the worst likely failure can be undone: read-only connections to curated content go first, and writes to anything leaving the company go last. Then weigh how many people benefit and whether the connection removes a step rather than adding one.

questions.question: Final pricing is sent to a customer and cannot be taken back once issued. Which oversight model fits?
options: Human-on-the-loop, with a supervisor watching for anomalies
Human-in-command only, with no review of individual outputs
No human review, because the system's accuracy record is strong
Human-in-the-loop, with a named person approving before release
questions.explanation: The bar is set by consequence and reversibility, so high stakes and hard-to-undo work needs a named sign-off before it leaves. Watching from above suits routine work where catching an occasional anomaly is enough.

questions.question: After a bad output, why should the explanation come before a low-stakes retry?
options: The explanation replaces any need for further use of the tool
The explanation gives the error a shape, and the retry rebuilds trust
The retry works only if the user first accepts that the tool is basically reliable
The order does not matter as long as both steps happen eventually
questions.explanation: An explanation converts a mystery into a navigable event, so the user knows the shape of the error. The retry then adds a small checkable win while the user stays in control of the output.

questions.question: An organization gives everyone access to an AI tool, but almost nobody uses it in daily work. What is that state?
options: Adoption, because every employee has been given access to the tool
An entitlement, because access exists without a change in how people work
A running program, because the licenses are already in place and paid for
A successful pilot, because usage has been tracked since the launch date
questions.explanation: Adoption means people actually use the tool and get value from it, so access without a change in behavior is only an entitlement.

questions.question: Why should a support network keep operating after the implementation project closes?
options: To take over the vendor relationship and contract talks from the project team
To reduce the number of licenses the company needs to buy
Because value leaks after go-live, and peers tied to the work catch it
To train the next group of managers in how the tool is meant to be used
questions.explanation: A share of value is lost after implementation, so peers tied to the daily work, not the project, are what keep the new way alive.

questions.question: In a scope section, why do the exclusions matter more than the inclusions?
options: They limit the program's budget to what the year can actually pay for
They let a team decline a request without having to escalate it for a ruling
They describe the systems the organization expects to connect during the year
They protect the program from any claim that it promised measurable results too early
questions.explanation: The exclusions are what let the organization say no inside its own operating model, without an escalation every time a request lands outside the year's scope. Inclusions describe intent, while exclusions carry authority.

questions.question: Why does a procurement-only inventory undercount the AI tools in use?
options: Tools bought on team cards, expensed individually, or bundled as upgrades never appear there
Procurement records list only the tools that passed a security review before they were purchased
Procurement systems delete the record once a subscription has been paid for in full
Free tools are left out because there is no purchase order for the system to record
questions.explanation: Buying now happens outside purchase orders and inside subscriptions the company already owns, so only charges, expense reports, and embedded tiers show what is really in use.

questions.question: Why does a voluntary survey on its own give an unreliable adoption picture?
options: People exaggerate how much they use AI in their daily work and overstate skill
People who rely on AI for important work often hide it, so the count runs low
Surveys reach too many people to analyze with any care
Surveys measure tools rather than the behavior they aim to capture
questions.explanation: When admitting AI use feels like a threat to job security, the heaviest users stay quiet, so disclosure has to be paired with observation.

questions.question: What does it tell you when one person can pause a use case, receives its failure reports, and explains it to leadership?
options: Whether the vendor has met its contractual security commitments
Whether every affected team has been consulted before launch
Whether the tool has passed a third-party security assessment
Whether one person with clear authority owns the case
questions.explanation: One name behind all three answers means real ownership; three different names with no path between them means the accountability is split and decisions will stall.

questions.question: What does classifying data as public, internal, confidential, or restricted let an owner do?
options: It replaces the need for a written acceptable use policy
It sets which data may enter a tool and on what terms
It proves the tool is safe enough to use without review
It ranks each identified threat by how likely it is to occur
questions.explanation: A classification draws a line people can actually follow, so use above the line is allowed and use below it needs a named rule instead of a vague warning to be careful.
